text: Picture a pill bug — the woodlouse under a flowerpot. Now make it a foot and a half long.
That's a giant isopod. A real relative of the pill bug, on the deep-sea floor.
Fourteen legs. And when it's bothered, it curls into a ball, just like its tiny cousin.
Even its eggs are huge: just over a centimetre across — among the biggest of any marine invertebrate.
A NOAA camera found one more than a thousand metres down, eating a fish head.
In captivity, some giant isopods have gone years without eating anything at all.
Then, when food finally comes, they gorge.
So how do you survive years with nothing to eat?
That trick is a type of its own. Every type of deep-sea creature is linked right here.
